title: Find Median From Data Stream
statement: Design a class that takes in numbers one at a time with addNum(num) and can return the median of everything added so far with findMedian(). The median is the middle value of the sorted numbers, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even.

example.caption: Add 3, 1, 2. The lower half holds the two smallest (1, 2) and the upper half holds 3. The count is odd, so the median is the lower top, 2.

output.label: lower half (max-heap). Top 2 is the median

idea.sentence: Split the numbers into a lower half in a max-heap and an upper half in a min-heap, so the median is always made from the two tops.

jargon.plain: The middle value of the sorted numbers. With an even count, the mean of the two middle values.
The lower half has the same size as the upper half, or one more. Then the middle is always at a top.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: operation names, then their arguments, e.g. ["MedianFinder","addNum","findMedian"], [[],[5],[]]

vars.meaning: how many numbers have been added

compare.bruteLabel: Re-sort everything, then read the middle
compare.optimalLabel: Two heaps, a few pushes and pops

rows.name: Keep a sorted array (insert in place)
rows.note: Binary search finds the spot, but inserting shifts up to n items.

rows.name: Two heaps
rows.note: Two or three heap operations per add. The median is read from the tops.

fast.takeaway: You never need the full order, only the border between the lower and upper halves. Two heaps keep exactly that border at their tops.

stages.title: Two empty heaps
stages.note: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.

stages.title: Add and cross over
stages.note: Push the number into the lower half, then move the lower half's biggest to the upper half. This keeps every lower number at most every upper number.

stages.title: Rebalance
stages.note: If the upper half became bigger, move its smallest back to the lower half. The lower half may hold one extra, never the upper.

stages.title: Read the median
stages.note: With an odd count, the median is the lower top. With an even count, it is the mean of both tops.

edges.title: One number
edges.why: The number crosses to the upper half, then is moved back to the lower. The lower holds the extra, so its top is the median.

edges.title: Two numbers
edges.why: Even count: the mean of the two tops, 1 and 2. The result is a float, so use true division.

edges.title: All equal
edges.why: Equal keys are fine. Which 4 ends in which heap does not matter.

edges.title: Negative numbers
edges.why: Only comparisons are used. Do not use 0 as a missing-value marker.

gotchas.text: The two-step add (push to lower, move its top to upper, then maybe move one back) is what keeps both the order and the sizes right. Pushing to either heap by guess breaks the order guarantee.

(a + b) / 2 is already a float in JavaScript. There is no integer division to worry about. There is also no built-in heap, so write a small one, and never sort inside findMedian because [10, 9, 100].sort() is lexicographic.
Integer division truncates: (3 + 4) / 2 is 3. Convert first: float64(a+b) / 2. For the max-heap, wrap minHeap and override only Less, so Len, Swap, Push and Pop are reused.
container/heap wants five methods: Len, Less, Swap, Push, Pop. heap.Pop returns any, but heap.Push takes any, so heap.Push(upper, heap.Pop(lower)) needs no type assertion.

recap.key: Max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half, sizes equal or lower one bigger. The median is at the tops.
recap.complexity: addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1). Space O(n).
moves: Push into lower, move lower's top to upper
If upper is bigger, move its top back to lower
Odd count: median is lower's top
Even count: mean of the two tops
